title: Antibody Dilution Calculator + 1:X Self-Test
description: Work out the antibody and diluent volumes for any 1:X dilution or working concentration, then test yourself on six questions taken from this page.
intro: Six questions on the dilutions above: what the number after the colon counts, where the diluent volume comes from, and when the volume is too small to pipette.

questions.q: The calculator opens at 1:1000 in a 5 mL final volume. What two volumes does it give?
questions.why: The factor divides the final volume to give the antibody, and the diluent is only what is left of that final volume, so the two have to add up to 5 mL rather than exceed it.
questions.source: Page defaults: ratio 1000, final volume 5 mL, so antibody = Vfinal / N = 5000 µL / 1000 = 5 µL and diluent = Vfinal − ab = 5000 − 5 = 4995 µL. The page FAQ states the same split: for 5 millilitres it is 5 microlitres of antibody plus 4995 microlitres. Computed by the page's calculator at runtime, not printed as static text.

questions.q: Under the convention this page uses, what does the 500 in 1:500 count?
options: 500 parts of buffer, plus one of stock
500 µL of stock in every millilitre
500 as a percentage of the final mix
questions.why: The number after the colon is the total parts, so 1:500 is one part antibody and 499 parts diluent, not one part added to 500 parts of buffer.
questions.source: Page section How antibody dilutions work: 'A dilution written as 1:500 means one part antibody in 500 parts total, not one part in 500 parts of diluent.' The FAQ repeats it: 1 part in 500 total, so 1 part antibody + 499 parts diluent.

questions.q: A datasheet gives a 1 mg/mL stock and recommends a 2 µg/mL working concentration. What dilution factor is that?
options: 1:1000, the stock figure on its own
questions.why: The factor is the stock divided by the working concentration in matching units, so the milligram stock has to be read as 1000 µg/mL before you divide.
questions.source: Page: 'A 1 mg/mL stock is 1000 µg/mL, so reaching 2 µg/mL needs 1000/2 = a 1:500 dilution.' The tool's concentration mode computes N = stock / work with the mg/mL option worth 1000. Recomputed: 1000 / 2 = 500.

questions.q: You need 1:5000 in 200 µL and your pipette will not go below 1 µL. What does this page have you do?
options: Pipette 0.04 µL and accept the error
Scale to 2 mL so 0.4 µL works
questions.why: Dilution factors multiply rather than add, so 1:100 followed by 1:50 reaches 1:5000 while keeping every volume above what a pipette can measure.
questions.source: Page section Why very high dilutions need two steps: '1:100  then  1:50  =  100 × 50  =  1:5000', for a 1:5000 in 200 µL that otherwise needs 0.04 µL. Recomputed: 200 / 5000 = 0.04, 100 × 50 = 5000, and 2000 / 5000 = 0.4, still under 1 µL.

questions.q: In that two-step example, step 2 makes the 200 µL of 1:5000. What goes into it?
options: 4 µL of neat stock plus 196 µL buffer
200 µL of the 1:100 and 4 µL buffer
4 µL of the 1:100 plus 196 µL buffer
2 µL of the 1:100 plus 198 µL buffer
questions.why: The second step dilutes the intermediate rather than the neat antibody, and the volume it needs is the final 200 µL divided by the second factor of 50.
questions.source: Page worked block: 'step 2   4 µL of that  + 196 µL diluent  → 200 µL of 1:5000'. Recomputed: 200 / 50 = 4 and 200 − 4 = 196.

questions.q: Which range does the page's table give as the typical starting point for a Western blot primary?
questions.why: Primaries sit roughly ten times more concentrated than the HRP secondary on the same table, so reading the wrong row wastes antibody or gives no signal at all.
questions.source: Page table Typical starting dilutions: Western blot primary 1:500 to 1:2000, Western blot secondary (HRP) 1:2000 to 1:10000, flow cytometry 1:50 to 1:200, immunofluorescence 1:200 to 1:1000.
